explanations.explanation: Shechem it is. Joshua assembles all the tribes there, plus the elders, leaders, judges and officers. That's a guest list that would make me hide my cookie boxes. Keep the name in your pocket, because Shechem shows up again at the very end of this chapter.
Gilgal is a real place in Israel's story. It's where they camped after crossing the Jordan (Joshua 4:19). This gathering isn't there, though. The text says Joshua assembled the tribes at Shechem.
Bethel is a place from Jacob's story, the spot he named in Genesis 28:19. Good name to know, friend, but it isn't on the map for this chapter. Joshua brings the tribes together at Shechem.

True. Joshua summoned the elders, leaders, judges and officers, and the text says, "…and they presented themselves before God." The tribes and their leaders are standing before Him at Shechem. I'd have checked my apron for flour first.

This one's true, baker. The text says Joshua summoned the elders, leaders, judges and officers, "…and they presented themselves before God." So the tribes and their leaders really do stand before God at Shechem. Big moment, and it hasn't even started yet.

Not quite, friend. The LORD says Israel's fathers, including Terah, lived beyond the Euphrates and worshiped other gods. So the story starts with a family that wasn't serving only the LORD. That makes what happens next even bigger.

False, and that's the honest answer. The LORD says Israel's fathers, including Terah, the father of Abraham and Nahor, lived beyond the Euphrates and worshiped other gods. He doesn't dress up where the family started. He just tells it straight, and that sets up everything else He says.
Isaac! The LORD says, "I gave him Isaac…" Abraham already had a son Ishmael (Genesis 16:15), so Isaac isn't his first child. But Isaac is the one the LORD names here, and He calls him a gift He gave.
Laban does show up later in the family story. He's the father of Leah and Rachel (Genesis 29:16). But he isn't who the LORD gives Abraham here. The text says, "I gave him Isaac…"

Jethro, Moses' father-in-law and the priest of Midian (Exodus 3:1), isn't in this part of the LORD's words. The LORD says, "I gave him Isaac…" Isaac is the answer, friend. Jethro's a fine name, I just can't make him fit.
Jacob goes in the first blank. The LORD says, "…to Isaac I gave Jacob and Esau." Two brothers, two paths. Esau got Mount Seir, and Jacob's line is the one this story follows.

Egypt goes in the second blank. The text says Jacob and his sons went down to Egypt. That's the place where this family's story takes a big turn, and the LORD brings them back out of it in the next verse.

Joseph is one of Jacob's sons (Genesis 35:24), not Isaac's. The first blank needs Esau's brother, and the LORD says, "…to Isaac I gave Jacob and Esau." Joseph does come back at the end of the chapter, when his bones are buried at Shechem.
Moab is a land with a king named Balak, and he shows up a little later in this very speech. But Jacob and his sons didn't go down to Moab. The text says they went down to Egypt.

Babylon isn't in this part of the LORD's words at all. Jacob and his sons went down to Egypt, and that's where the story goes from here. Good thing the Bible keeps its own map. I would have taken a wrong turn at the first oven.

Not quite, baker. The text tells us what the fathers did: "…your fathers cried out to the LORD…" Then the LORD acts. He puts darkness between them and the Egyptians and brings the sea over the Egyptians.

False. The text says Israel's fathers cried out to the LORD. Then He put darkness between them and the Egyptians, and brought the sea over the Egyptians. The crying out was theirs, and the rest was the LORD's doing.

Darkness. The LORD put darkness between Israel and the Egyptians. I know a little about darkness myself, from years stuck in the back of a junk drawer. But this was the LORD placing it between the camp of Egypt and the camp of Israel (Exodus 14:20).
Hail is a good guess for a dramatic moment, but the text doesn't say it here. The LORD put darkness between Israel and the Egyptians. Stick to what's written and the baking goes better.
Thunder would make a great sound effect, friend. But the text doesn't mention it at the Red Sea in this speech. It says the LORD put darkness between Israel and the Egyptians.
Curse. Balak sends for Balaam son of Beor to curse Israel. He wants words that work against them. The text tells us what Balak sent for, and in a moment we find out what he got.
Count is a nice, calm idea, baker, but it isn't what Balak wants. He sends for Balaam to curse Israel. Nobody's bringing a clipboard.
Warn would be gentler, but that's not the job. Balak, king of Moab, sends for Balaam son of Beor to curse Israel. He's after a curse, not a heads up.
It's the other way around, friend. The LORD says, "…I would not listen to Balaam." So Balaam doesn't curse Israel. He blesses them again and again.

False! The LORD says, "…I would not listen to Balaam. So he blessed you again and again, and I delivered you from his hand." Balak sent for Balaam to curse Israel and got blessings instead. That's like hiring a guy to boo your rival and watching him lead the cheering.

explanations.answer: The LORD delivers them into Israel's hand
explanations.explanation: That's it. The people of Jericho fought Israel, and so did the Amorites, Perizzites, Canaanites, Hittites, Girgashites, Hivites and Jebusites. The LORD says, "…I delivered them into your hand…" That's a long list of opponents with one ending.

explanations.answer: Israel makes a peace treaty with them
explanations.explanation: No treaty shows up in this speech. The LORD says the people of Jericho and those nations fought against Israel, and "…I delivered them into your hand…" He's the one who gets the credit.

explanations.answer: Israel retreats back across the Jordan
explanations.explanation: Israel crossed the Jordan and came to Jericho, and there's no turning back in the text. The LORD says that when all those nations fought them, "…I delivered them into your hand…" Nobody's packing up the cookie boxes and heading home.
Not so, baker. The LORD says the hornet drove out the two Amorite kings "…but not by your own sword or bow." He's telling Israel who did the work. It wasn't their weapons.

False. The LORD says, "I sent the hornet ahead of you, and it drove out the two Amorite kings before you, but not by your own sword or bow." So Israel wasn't the one swinging the win into place. He's making sure they know where it came from.

Yes. Joshua says to "cast aside the gods your fathers served beyond the Euphrates and in Egypt, and serve the LORD." He's telling them to throw out those old gods and serve only the LORD. Remember how this speech started, with fathers who worshiped other gods. It comes around.

Joshua doesn't say a word about riches, baker. What he wants cast aside is "…the gods your fathers served…" Treasure isn't on his list. Not that I'd be much help on riches anyway, since I started out with a 25 cent price sticker.

Weapons never come up in Joshua's charge. He tells them to cast aside "…the gods your fathers served beyond the Euphrates and in Egypt…" Gods are the only thing he names there. I'd have braced for a bigger list, friend.
That's the line. "As for me and my house, we will serve the LORD!" Joshua says it right after laying out the choice. He doesn't hide where he stands, and I love that.
Wait and see is not Joshua's style. After laying out the choice, he says, "As for me and my house, we will serve the LORD!" No hedging, no maybe.
Joshua doesn't point to the elders. He says, "As for me and my house, we will serve the LORD!" He answers for himself and his own house, plain and clear.

explanations.answer: He protected them throughout their journey
explanations.explanation: That's the one. The people say, "He also protected us throughout our journey and among all the nations through which we traveled." They look back and see the LORD with them all along the road. That's a pretty solid reason to stick with Him.

explanations.answer: He left them on their own after that
explanations.explanation: The people say the opposite, baker. They say He protected them throughout their journey and among all the nations they traveled through. After Egypt, they say He stayed with them.

explanations.answer: He gave them a king to lead them
explanations.explanation: No king shows up in what the people say. They name the LORD bringing them out of Egypt, the great signs, and how He protected them throughout their journey. Their reasons are all about what the LORD did.

explanations.answer: You are not able to serve the LORD
explanations.explanation: Joshua says, "You are not able to serve the LORD…" and he says it right after their big promise. Then he gives his reason: "…for He is a holy God; He is a jealous God…" I think Joshua wants them to feel how serious this promise is.

explanations.answer: The LORD is pleased with you today
explanations.explanation: Joshua doesn't say that. He tells them, "You are not able to serve the LORD, for He is a holy God…" It's a sobering answer to a big promise.

explanations.answer: You must first build Him an altar
explanations.explanation: An altar doesn't come up here. Joshua says, "You are not able to serve the LORD…" and then he talks about a holy and jealous God. His next instruction, later on, is to get rid of the foreign gods among them.
They don't back down, friend. Joshua tells them they can't, and the people reply, "No! We will serve the LORD!" Joshua's words don't change their promise.
False. The people reply, "No!" and then, "…we will serve the LORD!" Joshua tells them they can't, and they say it again anyway. That's a baker who hears "too hot" and grabs the oven mitts.

Witnesses. Joshua says, "You are witnesses against yourselves that you have chosen to serve the LORD." Their own words are on the record, and they're the ones who said them. It's like signing your own name on the cookie box.

Judges is a fair guess, since verse 1 names judges among the leaders gathered at Shechem. But Joshua's word here is witnesses. He says, "You are witnesses against yourselves that you have chosen to serve the LORD."
Strangers doesn't fit, baker. These are the people who just promised to serve the LORD. Joshua says, "You are witnesses against yourselves that you have chosen to serve the LORD."
They don't refuse, friend. When Joshua says it, the people answer, "We are witnesses!" They agree, and they own what they said.
False. The people don't refuse, they agree. Joshua says, "You are witnesses against yourselves…" and the people reply, "We are witnesses!" That's a yes to their own promise.

explanations.answer: They will serve the LORD and obey His voice
explanations.explanation: That's what they say: "We will serve the LORD our God and obey His voice." Notice the new part, obeying His voice. Joshua told them to get rid of the foreign gods and incline their hearts, and this is their answer.

explanations.answer: They will think it over until morning
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't give them until morning. The people say to Joshua, "We will serve the LORD our God and obey His voice." Nobody asks for a timer.

explanations.answer: They will decide once each tribe meets
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't send them off to separate meetings. The people say to Joshua, "We will serve the LORD our God and obey His voice." It's one answer, right there at Shechem.
Stone. Joshua takes a large stone and sets it up under the oak near the sanctuary of the LORD. It gives the people something they can see. Next, he tells them what that rock is for.
An altar is a holy thing (Exodus 29:37), so it's a natural guess. But the text says Joshua took a large stone and set it up under the oak. No altar here.

A lampstand is something the LORD told Moses to make of pure gold (Exodus 25:31). Here, though, Joshua takes a large stone and sets it up under the oak near the sanctuary of the LORD. Plain old stone, friend.

explanations.answer: It has heard all the LORD's words to them
explanations.explanation: Yes. Joshua says, "You see this stone. It will be a witness against us, for it has heard all the words the LORD has spoken to us…" That's his reason. Anyone can walk up and look at it, and it stands there as a reminder.

explanations.answer: It was carried up from the Jordan
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't say where the stone came from. Joshua's reason is that it has heard all the words the LORD has spoken to them. That's why it will be a witness.

explanations.answer: Moses carved the Law into it
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't say anything is carved on this stone. Joshua recorded these things in the Book of the Law of God, then set the stone up. He says it will be a witness because it has heard all the LORD's words.
110 is right. Joshua son of Nun died at the age of 110, and the text calls him "…the servant of the LORD…" right where it tells of his death. I think that's a title worth having on the last page.
120 is the age Moses died, Israel's leader before Joshua (Deuteronomy 34:7). Close, but Joshua was 110. The text says he died at the age of 110.
175 is the age Abraham died, the father of Israel's family (Genesis 25:7). That's a big number, friend. Joshua died at 110.

True. The text says, "Israel had served the LORD throughout the days of Joshua and of the elders who outlived him and who had experienced all the works that the LORD had done for Israel." It names two stretches: Joshua's days, and the days of those elders. The promise at Shechem held that long.

The text says it did hold, baker. Israel served the LORD throughout the days of Joshua and of the elders who outlived him. Those were the people who had experienced all the works the LORD had done for Israel. So the answer is true.
